Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network? · Platforms · Lex Plataformae
<1>Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network?</1><2>Infrastructure and intermediation IOCs</2>

You look for a product in an online store, compare prices, check the reviews and pick the seller who seems most reliable. Or you open a social network and see what is trending, what others liked and what seems to matter that day.

It feels like you are looking at the market or the conversation as they are. But everything reached you already selected, ordered and highlighted by the platform, using criteria you do not control and can almost never check.
The market, the offer and even the social relevance of what circulates within it reach the consumer and the user through private filters of visibility, salience and intelligibility.<1>p. 761</1>
It does not matter what was sold in the end or what sector the platform works in. What decides is how it organizes the exchange, the meeting and the comparison inside the environment it runs.
These platforms usually present themselves as a neutral square that merely brings sellers and buyers together, or those who post and those who read. That is true only on the surface.
What you get is a structure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and delivery. Without it, the product or the content would not even have reached you the way it did.

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption on infrastructure and intermediation platforms is defined neither by the final object traded nor by the traditional economic classification of the sector in which the platform operates.<1>p. 760</1>

In their formal language, they often appear as neutral spaces of encounter between seller and buyer, between sender and receiver, between advertiser and audience, between content producers and the public.<1>p. 761</1>
This description, although partly true on a superficial level, is insufficient to capture the real structure of supply.<1>p. 761</1>
Why is the storefront part of what you get?

You do not consume only a third party's product or the post that shows up on your screen. Before that, you consume the frame that defines what seems most relevant, most reliable, safest, most popular or most worthy of attention.

That is why rankings, reputation, featured spots, recommendations and reach are not screen details. They are part of the platform's usefulness and weigh on what you expect, on the risk you see and on the choice you make.
Before that, they consume private frames that define what will be seen as most relevant, most reliable, most comparable, safest, most popular or most worthy of attention.<1>p. 761</1>
Where does this show up in your daily life?

<1>In online stores.</1> The terms of use of the big marketplaces show that the platform organizes much more than listings. It handles the rules, visibility, payment, reputation, delivery and dispute resolution.
<1>On social networks.</1> The terms of the big networks show private rules on what stays up, who sees what, what gets moderated and how the conversation circulates.
Shopping and conversation are different things, but the mechanism is the same. In both cases, the platform governs the place where things appear and prepares the space in which you will decide.
In both cases, the platform does not merely host listings. It administers criteria of presentation, trust, prioritization and legibility of the market accessible to the consumer.<1>p. 762</1>

Here too the platform does not merely “let” content produced by third parties “appear”. It administers the way this content enters the user's field of perception and how its relevance is socially stabilized.<1>p. 762</1>
In both cases, the platform governs the environment of appearance.<1>p. 762</1>
Do you really choose on your own?
You do not choose in front of a transparent market, with every offer side by side. You choose inside a field the platform has already interpreted for you.

Your choice is shaped by how prominently an item is placed, how trustworthy a seller looks, the way reviews are displayed and the difference between what is sponsored and what is not. It is also shaped by the link to payment and delivery and by the order of categories.
In the end, the platform produces the market you are able to see.

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it grows because the platform's screen starts to manufacture what is real for you, and what it does not show almost ceases to exist.
It is a semiotic vulnerability intensified by structural dependence on the interface as the producer of the accessible real.<1>p. 763</1>
What does the platform promise without saying it?

The promise is not only in what the company says out loud, like neutrality, efficiency or convenience. It is also in the implicit promise that you will be able to make sense of the market or the conversation that appears on the screen.

When the criteria are hidden, when there are internal interests you do not see or when the order of things cannot be checked, what you get is hit at its core. You lose the ability to read the environment.

In environments like these, the supplier's promise lies not only in the explicit discourse of neutrality, efficiency or convenience. It also lies in the implicit promise that the market or social circulation will be intelligible.<1>p. 763</1>

When this intelligibility is governed by opaque criteria, non-transparent internal interests or non-auditable ranking patterns, enjoyment comes to be affected in its very core of legibility.<1>p. 763</1>
Looking at the product that arrived or the post that vanished is not enough. The whole experience has to be reconstructed. Depending on the case, that means looking at the following.
How the offers were presented.
What was a paid result and what was not.
The role of reviews and reputation.
The link between prominence and delivery.
The badges and trust signals on the screen.
The context in which the content appeared and the moderation rules.

On a social network, it also matters how the feed, recommendations and reach shaped what you saw. In an online store, what matters is the ranking, featured placement, seller rating and sponsorship. Keep dated screenshots while you still can.

This includes, depending on the case, the way offers are presented, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of reviews and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the signals of reliability provided by the interface, the context in which content appears, the relevant moderation criteria and the mechanisms through which the platform induces a perception of market, consensus or priority.<1>p. 763</1>
<1>Thinking the screen is just decoration.</1> The way things are shown is part of what the platform supplies.
<1>Thinking the platform answers only for what it wrote.</1> What it actually does with visibility also counts, and not just what is in the contract or the advertising.
<1>Thinking the problem is only the last step.</1> The failed purchase or the removed post is the end of a story. What led there was the storefront the platform set up.
These traps leave the platform with all the power over your choice, hidden behind an appearance of neutral technique.

The second is the tendency to imagine that the platform would only be legally answerable for what it expressly stated in a clause or in advertising, as if the effective governance of visibility were legally irrelevant.<1>p. 763</1>

The third is the tendency to reduce the dispute to the terminal act, such as the failed purchase, the removal of content or the supposed preference for a given offer, without investigating the private structure of salience that conditioned the user's entire experience.<1>p. 763</1>
What must the platform guarantee?
No one can demand that the platform open up all its systems. But it has to make the minimum checkable about how it presents, ranks, moderates and rates what appears.

What is asked for is enough clarity for you to understand how the environment organizes your experience, and how the platform's choices weigh on what you expect, on how you compare offers and on your chance to challenge them.

What is demanded is sufficient intelligibility to understand how the environment organizes the user's experience and how certain choices of the platform interfere with the formation of expectation, the comparability of alternatives and the possibility of challenge.<1>p. 764</1>
And if the platform changes the rules of the game?

Sometimes the platform changes how it intermediates, the logic of who gets seen, the reputation criteria or the rules of circulation. If the change makes what you legitimately had much worse and nothing makes up for the loss, it may be challenged.
This applies to those who buy and sell in the online store and to those who post and seek reach on the social network.

This can occur both in e-commerce and in the social circulation of content, whenever the platform substantially alters the functional role of the infrastructure it offered as an environment of exchange, reach or recognition.<1>p. 764</1>

The path is to demand duties about the very way things are organized, and not just to argue about the final product or about what a third party did. It is fair to ask whether it was clear what the platform was doing there and whether sponsored content could be told apart from the rest.

It is also fair to ask whether the reputation shown could be checked and whether hidden criteria got in the way of comparison. And whether the screen itself misled, confused or created an imbalance that consumer law does not accept.
In the most serious cases, when the same company referees the storefront and profits from what happens in it, the issue may reach broader abusive practices and competition among sellers.
Did your choice depend on what the platform highlighted, hid or ranked?
Was it unclear what was a paid ad or how reputation was calculated?
Did the platform change the visibility or reputation rules without explaining?

The subtype thus shows that the infrastructure and intermediation platform is not a mere neutral corridor through which previously formed wills circulate. It is an agent in building the field in which those wills become possible, perceptible and actionable.<1>p. 764</1>
